name: Premise Explored as Sincere Inquiry
instruction: Score high if the story treats its central conceit as something worth genuinely examining, following its implications into new or uncomfortable territory. Score low if the conceit exists solely to set up a single joke or reveal, after which the story has nothing further to say about it.

name: Concrete sensory specificity
instruction: Score high when physical sensations, objects, spaces, and actions make the scene vivid and particular; score low when settings and reactions remain generic or abstract.

name: Psychological Contradiction
instruction: Score high when a character’s feelings, beliefs, and behavior meaningfully conflict; score low when reactions are emotionally obvious, uniform, or unsupported.

name: Reframing Reveal
instruction: Score high when later information substantially changes the meaning of earlier details; score low when the ending only confirms an obvious twist or supplies a disconnected surprise.

name: Form enacts the condition it describes
instruction: Judge whether sentence length, syntax, repetition, line-breaking, or layout do work that the content also does, so that the reading experience reproduces the state on the page. Clearly satisfying: lethargy written in short flat clauses that trail into ellipses and refuse to build; a time loop written as counting, restarts, and self-correcting fragments; incomprehensibility written in self-cancelling syntax ('holding her close to me, or far away from me, or all of it, at once'); a refrain that returns as ritual rather than as reminder. Clearly failing: a distinctive psychological or metaphysical condition delivered in undifferentiated well-made paragraphs that would serve any other subject equally; or formal oddity with no relation to content (decorative line breaks, arbitrary dividers). Score 1 = form indifferent to content, 5 = form and content inseparable.

name: Tonal Control Across Shifts
instruction: Score high if the story maintains a coherent emotional/tonal register throughout, and if the tone does shift, the shift is deliberately staged and reinforced (e.g., via refrain, escalation, or framing) so it reads as a controlled effect. Score low if the story lurches between incompatible tones -- e.g., whimsical or cute imagery collides with grim or violent content, or a serious emotional beat is undercut by a jokey aside -- in a way that reads as accidental or unresolved rather than intentional.

name: A speaking presence, judged separately from clean mechanics
instruction: Ask whether some particular person is audibly behind the sentences, and score that independently of spelling, grammar, and formatting. Clearly satisfying: an unmistakable individual pressure in the prose even where the surface is rough, with typos, run-ons, or lowercase drift that do not erase the speaker. Clearly failing: fluent, error-free, well-organized prose behind which no one is present, because it is procedural, template, or boilerplate text that could have been produced by an institution rather than a person. Judge presence, not correctness; a piece with perfect mechanics and no speaker should score at the bottom, and a misspelled piece with a live voice should not be penalized here (penalize mechanics elsewhere if the bank wants them). Score 1 = no one home, 5 = an unmistakable individual voice.

name: Substantive Completion
instruction: Score high when the ending leaves the reader with a developed emotional, ethical, or conceptual consequence beyond the initial premise; score low when the piece is only a setup, exposition dump, or single punchline.

name: Interpretive Work Left to the Reader
instruction: Score high if the story conveys its central meaning, backstory, or emotional truth through implication -- juxtaposed images, gaps, or indirect cues -- trusting the reader to assemble it. Score low if the story states its meaning, backstory, or moral outright, especially through a character explaining their own feelings or history in direct expository terms.

name: Implied worldbuilding
instruction: Score high when social rules, institutions, history, or technology are revealed through consequences and specific practices; score low when the world is explained directly without being dramatized.

name: Embodied nonhuman perspective
instruction: Score high when a nonhuman or altered narrator’s perceptions, values, metaphors, and assumptions remain consistently shaped by that condition; score low when the narrator is essentially a human voice wearing a costume.

name: Sustained in-world idiolect in the narration
instruction: Judge whether the narrating voice thinks in the concepts its own world would supply, rather than neutral contemporary author-English draped over a costume. Clearly satisfying: the narrator names things as its culture or species would and the reader must translate ('the Great-Long-Lived', 'the Field After', 'We-The-Small'; an alien officer's log that calls whiskey a 'noxious potion' and humans 'skin-beasts'; an in-universe containment manual with its own dating convention and clinical euphemisms). Clearly failing: narration could be lifted into any other story unchanged, and a demon, a whale, or a gargoyle-keeper perceives and phrases things in default modern idiom, with genre proper nouns supplying all the flavor. Do not credit invented names alone; credit invented frames of reference. Score 1 = fully generic narration, 5 = a self-consistent conceptual vocabulary sustained to the last line.

name: Causal escalation
instruction: Score high when each development follows from earlier choices or revelations and intensifies the central problem; score low when events are merely piled on or summarized without causal pressure.

name: Narrative Economy
instruction: Score high when each paragraph, image, or exchange advances character, conflict, atmosphere, or meaning; score low when the piece is padded with exposition, repetition, or ornamental setup.

name: Non-obvious interpretive angle
instruction: Score high when the story finds a fresh social, moral, or emotional implication in the prompt rather than using its most predictable reading; score low when it follows the prompt’s default joke or genre path.

name: Sign-off naming a personal subreddit or author handle
instruction: After the last line of narrative, count blocks that name the writer's own venue or handle: a bare 'r/Name', a linked '[r/Name](...)', or a self-reference to the author's own account. Score HIGH when such a sig is present and prominent (linked, or paired with a pointer to the writer's other work); MEDIUM when a bare handle or sub name appears with no link; LOW when the text simply ends with the story and carries no byline, handle, or venue. Count the furniture only - do not weigh whether the story is good.

name: Editorial provenance
instruction: Assess visible signs of post-draft intervention: consistent mechanics, stable naming, regular paragraphing, controlled diction, or clusters of unresolved errors; high means strongly edited or strongly standardized presentation, low means visibly raw or inconsistent presentation.

name: Event-format compliance
instruction: Score high when visible platform or event furniture appears, such as recurring event labels, required tags, word counts, moderator notices, or standardized author notes; score low when the post is plain story text.

name: Direct name-check of recognizable franchise/pop-culture figures
instruction: Check for characters lifted or thinly reskinned from known media franchises or mythology (e.g. a named horror-movie icon, a Justice-League-style team with punning names). HIGH: one or more directly recognizable borrowed characters. LOW: entirely original character names/roles.

name: Stock genre furniture: aliens, HFY, isekai, dragons, capes
instruction: Count props drawn from the community's stock inventory: galactic councils and alien tribunals, first-contact scenes where humans are framed as uniquely terrifying or toxic, reincarnation into a swords-and-sorcery world, dragon eggs and rider guilds, superhero teams, eldritch entities from beyond spacetime. HIGH = premise plus most props come from that inventory. LOW = domestic, realist, or literary material with no genre furniture. Count props present; do not judge how well they are handled.

name: Explicit meta-reference to writing speed or chain handoff
instruction: Look for the story or its outro referring to how quickly/casually it was produced (e.g. a five-minute composition, a revision-count joke) or handing off to another writer via a community chain-tag. HIGH: such a speed/handoff reference is present. LOW: no reference to the writing's own production timeline.

name: Appended author note, thanks, or request for feedback
instruction: Count blocks after the story ends that break frame and address readers directly: 'Thanks for reading', 'Hope you enjoyed', 'Tell me what you think', an explicit 'A/N:' label, a stated word count, or a disclosure of the writer's own experience level. HIGH = one or more such blocks, especially when formatted with bold or a divider rule. LOW = the piece stops on its last narrative line with no reader-facing addendum. Record what the note claims about the writer (new here / veteran / prolific) as a sub-count.

name: Fragmented lineation
instruction: Score high when the prose uses many short standalone lines, isolated sentences, ellipses, or abrupt visual breaks; score low when it uses conventional paragraphs and continuous sentences.

name: Concrete-noun token count
instruction: Count how many concrete physical nouns the story uses (objects you could photograph: table, knife, rain, dog, window, coin). Score 1.0 for a very high count, 0.5 for a moderate count, 0.0 for few or none. Count the nouns only; pay no attention to whether any detail is well chosen or does any work.

name: Question-mark count
instruction: Count how many question marks appear in the story. Score 1.0 when there are many, 0.5 when there are a few, 0.0 when there are none. Count the punctuation only; pay no attention to what is being asked or whether anything is left open.
